--- license: apache-2.0 license_link: https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0 pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text tags: - conversational - image-text-to-text - moe library_name: transformers --- # Inkling 2 Mini

Playground | Tinker Cookbook

## 1. General Information Inkling 2 Mini is a general-purpose multimodal model that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is intended for use in English and other languages, and across multiple coding languages. The model is designed to be used by developers building AI-powered applications, including agentic and tool-use systems, coding assistants, chatbots, and retrieval-augmented generation systems, and is suitable for general-purpose conversational use, instruction-following, and other natural language and visual tasks. It is released with open weights to support research, fine-tuning and integration into third-party products by downstream developers. **Languages:** English, general multilingual support **Model provider:** Thinking Machines Lab, Inc. **Date of release:** November 20, 2026 **License:** Apache 2.0 [Model Acceptable Use Policy](https://thinkingmachines.ai/model-acceptable-use-policy/) ## 2. Getting Started The weights are available for download through Hugging Face [here](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini). Developers can also access the model using the Tinker fine-tuning platform, which provides API access. * For accessing our model via Tinker, you can get started by referring to the Tinker Cookbook [here](https://github.com/thinking-machines-lab/tinker-cookbook), and installing the tml-renderers package [here](https://pypi.org/project/tml-renderers/). * Tinker playground also provides inference-only access to the model [here](https://tinker.thinkingmachines.ai/playground). ### Required hardware The model is distributed as a single checkpoint of about 20GB, in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 precisions. Given its small size, it is possible to run this checkpoint on local AI compute for inference. We support: * 1x NVIDIA DGX Spark * Apple silicon devices with 32GB or more memory (MacBooks, Mac minis and Studios) * Other GPUs and platforms are possible, with 32GB or more of VRAM recommended ### Required software Inkling 2 Mini supports local inference using the following frameworks, along with their dependency libraries: * [Hugging Face](https://hf.co/blog/inkling2mini) * [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/ThinkingMachines/Inkling-2-Mini) * [vLLM](https://recipes.vllm.ai/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini) * [TokenSpeed](https://lightseek.org/tokenspeed/recipes/models#inkling-2-mini) * NVIDIA Dynamo * [Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/inkling-2-mini), including quantized GGUF versions * llama.cpp, for quantized GGUF versions * [Llama App](https://llama.app/) * Ollama and Exo Labs, on Apple silicon Inkling 2 Mini can also be post-trained with: * [Miles](https://miles.radixark.com/docs/models/thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini) * [SkyRL](https://docs.skyrl.ai/docs/models/inkling2) ## 3. Model Properties ### Model type Multimodal autoregressive looped transformer ### Architecture type A 24-layer decoder-only transformer with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layers. The middle 12 layers run three times with shared weights, giving 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights. In each layer, each token is routed to 8 of 128 experts. Attention is a hybrid of local and global layers. The model is natively multimodal – images are encoded via a vision transformer – with image and text inputs projected into a shared hidden space and processed jointly by the decoder. ### Parameters 26.4B, 3.4B active Note: each extra pass through the looped layers adds about 1.0B effective active parameters. Since the model runs with three passes, there are 5.4B effective active parameters per token. ### Numerics support NVFP4 and MXFP8 ### Input modalities * Text: UTF-8 encoded text * Image: Any pixel-based image input. For optimal performance, each image dimension should be between 40px to 4096px. Inkling 2 Mini supports a context window of up to 1M tokens. ### Output modalities Text ## 4. Training Training data includes a broad variety of content types, including text, images, video. Training data for the model was drawn from publicly available sources, acquired from third-parties, generated internally, or synthetically generated or augmented. Publicly available data includes content from the public internet and publicly accessible repositories. Data curation includes cleaning, processing, and modifying datasets. These processing steps, which vary by data type, may include deduplication and filtering to remove junk or other low-quality data, or to advance safety or other objectives. ## 5. Evaluations

--- ## Table of Contents - [Model Introduction](#model-introduction) - [Pretrained model capability](#pretrained-model-capability) - [Practicality and Cost Efficiency](#practicality-and-cost-efficiency) - [Optimization Approach](#optimization-approach) - [Task Performance and Cost](#task-performance-and-cost) - [User Blind Evaluation](#user-blind-evaluation) - [Appendix: Benchmark results](#appendix-benchmark-results) - [News](#news) - [Model Links](#model-links) - [Quickstart](#quickstart) - [Transformers](#transformers) - [OpenAI-compatible API](#openai-compatible-api) - [Deployment](#deployment) - [DFly2 for Speculative Decoding](#dfly2-for-speculative-decoding) - [Quantization](#quantization) - [Inference Frameworks](#inference-frameworks) - [vLLM](#vllm) - [SGLang](#sglang) - [Finetuning](#finetuning) - [License](#license) - [Contact Us](#contact-us) ## Model Introduction **Hy4 flash** is our most cost-effective Hy model to date, featuring 220B total parameters (including 64B Engram parameters) with just 12B active parameters per token. It natively accepts text and image inputs, generates text, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens. Its 42-layer language backbone consists of one dense feed-forward layer and 41 MoE layers, with identity Hyper-Connections (iHC) supporting inter-layer information flow. A vision encoder (adapted from SigLIP2-So400m-Patch16-Res512) is connected to the backbone through an MLP projector. In addition to the backbone, a built-in 5-layer drafter, [DFly2](#dfly2-for-speculative-decoding) (0.85B parameters), reuses the target model's KV cache and sparse indices to support long-context speculative decoding at a low, constant cost. Compared with Hy4, Hy4 Flash introduces three notable architectural changes: 1. **Hybrid attention.** Sparse attention (IndexPool) and sliding-window attention (SWA) are interleaved at a 1:3 ratio. 2. **LatentMoE.** Routed experts operate in a lower-dimensional latent space. Each token activates 16 of 512 routed experts, alongside one shared expert. 3. **N-gram embedding (Engram).** The backbone is augmented with learned bigram and trigram representations, retrieved via multi-head hash lookups. | Property | Value | | --- | --- | | **Overview** | | | Architecture | Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) | | Total Parameters (excluding Engram, ViT, and DFly2) | 155.5B | | Engram --- license: apache-2.0 library_name: inworld-voice-isolation pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio tags: [audio, speech, speech-enhancement, speech-denoising, noise-suppression, voice-isolation, 48khz, full-band, streaming, realtime] ---

Voice Isolator

Open-license (Apache-2.0) 48 kHz voice isolation for noisy speech recordings and live audio.

--- ## TL;DR Inworld Voice Isolator v1 ships as two models that share one architecture: | | `voice-isolator-v1` | `voice-isolator-v1-realtime` | |---|---|---| | made for | recorded audio and anything not latency-sensitive, at the best quality | live audio, as a stream in your pipeline or production | | how it runs | offline: every frame sees its whole 8 s chunk | a causal stream with 20 ms of look-ahead | | parameters | 64M | 58M | **Use them for** cleaning recordings before playback or publication, curating speech datasets and voice pipelines where the speaker's identity must survive. With the realtime model, use them for live calls and streams. Subtract the isolated voice from the input to extract background noise or a backing-track residual for vocals/music separation. **They are not** a speaker selector or a restoration model. Restoration is planned for version 2 (see [Plans](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator#plans)). ## Quick start Using a coding agent? Point it at the [setup section of AGENTS.md](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/blob/main/AGENTS.md#setting-up-the-voice-isolator-for-a-user): it installs the package, checks the machine with `voice-isolate-doctor` and cleans a first file. ```bash pip install inworld-voice-isolation # or from a clone: git clone https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator && cd voice-isolator && pip install -e . # a noisy example; a clone also has it at demo/examples/sample_14.wav curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/main/demo/examples/sample_14.wav # offline isolation (downloads the offline model on first use): # the voice goes to sample_14_clean.wav and the removed background # to sample_14_clean_background.wav, beside it voice-isolate sample_14.wav sample_14_clean.wav ``` Both are float32 WAVs at 48 kHz, with their original levels preserved; together they reconstruct the aligned mono input. Use `--output-sr 0` to keep the input rate, `--background noise.wav` to choose the background path for one file, or `--no-background` to save only the voice. ```python from inworld import voice_isolation # isolate a recording offline offline = voice_isolation.VoiceIsolator("inworld/voice-isolator") wav, sample_rate = voice_isolation.load_audio("sample_14.wav") voice = offline.isolate(wav, sample_rate) voice_isolation.save_audio("sample_14_clean.wav", voice, sample_rate, subtype="FLOAT") voice_isolation.save_audio("sample_14_clean_background.wav", wav - voice, sample_rate, subtype="FLOAT") # what was removed ``` ### Streaming The realtime model isolates the voice as the audio arrives, with 20 ms of look-ahead: ```python import torch from inworld import voice_isolation live = voice_isolation.VoiceIsolator("inworld/voice-isolator", mode="streaming", lookahead_frames=2) session = live.stream() # takes 48 kHz mono, in pieces of any size wav, sample_rate = voice_isolation.load_audio("sample_14.wav") # 48 kHz mono, standing in for a live source voice = [] for start in range(0, len(wav), 960): # 20 ms at a time, as a microphone delivers it voice.append(session.push(wav[start:start + 960])) # the samples that are final: play or send them voice.append(session.flush()) # the rest, once the source ends voice_isolation.save_audio("sample_14_streamed.wav", torch.cat(voice), sample_rate) ``` The streaming CLI writes only the isolated voice, after the whole file has gone through: ```bash voice-isolate sample_14.wav sample_14_streamed.wav --mode streaming --lookahead 2 ``` The weights download on first use, and their checksums are verified. The mode picks the checkpoint: `voice-isolator-v1` offline, `voice-isolator-v1-realtime` for streaming. CUDA is used when available, Apple's Metal backend (`mps`) on an Apple-silicon Mac with PyTorch 2.6 or later, and the CPU otherwise; `--device` picks one. The code, the [interactive demo](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/blob/main/demo/README.md) and the [benchmark](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/blob/main/bench/README.md) are on GitHub: [inworld-ai/voice-isolator](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator). The demo loads both models at startup: **Offline** processes files and samples into voice and background audio; **Online** streams the microphone for up to 60 seconds with updating waveforms and spectrograms, pausing capture before playback. ## Hardware Tested on NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (A100, H100, B200 and B300) and on CPU. Smaller GPUs are not tested yet (see [Plans](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator#plans)). ## The VIBE benchmark

# FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency

[![Project Page](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project-Page-green)](https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-fastframes/)
[![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2611.23226-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23226)
[![FastFrames-S](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97_Model-FastFrames--S-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/apple/FastFrames-S)
[![FastFrames-L](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97_Model-FastFrames--L-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/apple/FastFrames-L)
[![Community Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97_Space-Community_Demo-blue)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/akhaliq/FastFrames-L)

This repository contains the official implementation of *FastFrames: Video Generation at
Interactive Latency*. We release [FastFrames-S](https://huggingface.co/apple/FastFrames-S)
(1.3B) and [FastFrames-L](https://huggingface.co/apple/FastFrames-L) (14B). Both are
autoregressive, two-step video diffusion models that generate 480p video at interactive
latency. We also release an optimized version of LingBot 1.3B that is 16x faster than the
official model and allows fluid camera-conditioned control.

- [Latency profiling](#latency-profiling)
- [Interactive demo with LingBot](#interactive-demo-with-lingbot)
- [T2V generation](#t2v-generation)
- [VBench evaluation](#vbench-evaluation)
- [Training](#training)
- [Citation](#citation)

[![FastFrames demo: LingBot camera control with and without FastFrames optimizations](assets/fastframes_demo_preview.gif)](assets/fastframes_demo.mp4)

## Installation

Linux x86-64 with an NVIDIA GPU and a CUDA 12.8-compatible driver. From the repository root:

```bash
uv sync
```

Download FastFrames and third-party weights using the [checkpoint guide](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/docs/installation.md#checkpoints).

## Latency Profiling

```bash
uv run python evaluation/latency/benchmark.py ff-s
uv run python evaluation/latency/benchmark.py ff-l --gpus 8
```

Example component timings for **FastFrames-S, 1 GPU, 480p**, with a full KV cache.

| Component | Calls | Latency per call | Total latency |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| DiT evaluation, t=1000 | 1 | 16.1 ms | 16.1 ms |
| DiT evaluation, t=833 | 1 | 16.2 ms | 16.2 ms |
| KV refinement | 1 | 2.2 ms | 2.2 ms |
| Pixel decoder | 1 | 0.9 ms | 0.9 ms |
| **Total** | | | **35.4 ms** (paper: 36 ms) |

See the [profiling guide](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/docs/inference.md#profiling) for details and baselines.

## Interactive Demo with LingBot

Complete the [demo setup](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/docs/lingbot.md#interactive-demo-13b), then launch one of:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 uv run --extra lingbot --extra demo python apps/lingbot/demo.py --gpus 1
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 uv run --extra lingbot --extra demo python apps/lingbot/demo.py --gpus 8
```

and open `http://localhost:8000`.

## T2V Generation

```bash
uv run python scripts/generate.py --model ff-s --checkpoint-dir checkpoints \
    --prompt "A corgi surfing a wave at sunset" --seed 0 --output outputs/corgi.mp4
```

Outputs 832 × 480 video, 81 frames at 16 fps. Use `--model ff-l` for FastFrames-L.

To generate the videos on our project page (20+ videos):

```bash
uv run python scripts/generate_project_page.py --model ff-s --output-dir outputs/project_page/ff-s
uv run python scripts/generate_project_page.py --model ff-l --output-dir outputs/project_page/ff-l
```

See the [generation guide](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/docs/inference.md#generation) for details.

## VBench Evaluation

Follow the [evaluation guide](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/docs/inference.md#evaluation) to reproduce Table 1's
Quality / Semantic / Total scores.

## Training

### [Causal Forcing++ -> FastFrames-S](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/docs/training.md#causal-forcing---fastframes-s)

FastFrames-S keeps the two-step frame-wise Causal Forcing++ generator frozen and trains the
networks around it.

### [Wan2.1-14B -> FastFrames-L](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/docs/training.md#wan21-14b---fastframes-l)

We first distill Wan2.1-14B into a two-step causal model following the Causal Forcing++ recipe,
then train its pixel decoder and KV refinement network as for FastFrames-S. We release all
checkpoints: 1) a causal teacher trained on latents generated by Wan2.1-14B; 2) the
consistency-distilled model; 3) the DMD-distilled model; 4) the final generator, pixel decoder
and KV refinement network.

## Citation

If you find this work useful in your research, please cite:

```bibtex
@article{chou2026fastframes,
  title   = {FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency},
  author  = {Chou, Gene and Yang, Guandao and Luan, Fujun and Mescheder, Lars and
             Dong, Wei and Richter, Stephan R. and Koltun, Vladlen},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2611.23226},
  year    = {2026}
}
```

## License and Acknowledgments

LingBot-World v2 code and weights follow their upstream [CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/LICENSE_LINGBOT).
All other FastFrames code is licensed under the [Apple Sample Code License](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/LICENSE).
Also see [ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-fastframes/blob/main/ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS) for third-party code.

We thank the authors of [Wan2.1](https://github.com/Wan-Video/Wan2.1),
[Self-Forcing](https://github.com/guandeh17/Self-Forcing), and
[Causal Forcing++](https://github.com/thu-ml/Causal-Forcing) for releasing their code, on which the
FastFrames code and models build.

--- base_model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B library_name: peft license: apache-2.0 datasets: - harness-hub/scale800-harbor - harness-hub/harness-adapters - harness-hub/termgrade-train-harbor - ai-and/termgrade-environments tags: - trl - grpo - async-grpo - lora - agents - harbor - openenv - pi pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text --- ![](banner.png) A LoRA adapter for [Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B), trained with reinforcement learning to work as the model behind the [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) coding agent on software-engineering and terminal tasks. > [!Tip] > **Most of the gain of maximum-effort thinking, at a quarter of the tokens.** With thinking off, this adapter > matches the base model thinking at its highest reasoning effort (`xhigh`) on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (56.6% vs 54.2%), > and gets 25 of thinking's 35 points on SWE-bench Pro (64.7% vs 74.5%), while generating about 4.5× fewer tokens per > task. See [Thinking vs no thinking](#thinking). - **SWE-bench Pro (hard 51):** 39.2% → 64.7% (+25.5 points; 15 tasks newly solved, 2 lost). - **Terminal-Bench 2.1:** 39.5% → 55.8% (+16.3 points; 16 newly solved, 2 lost). - **Close to thinking-level accuracy, without thinking:** level with the base model at its highest reasoning effort on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 10 points behind on SWE-bench Pro, with about 4.5× fewer generated tokens. - **Less work per task:** under half the turns of the base model on the tasks both solve. > [!Note] > All results are under the pi harness: one attempt per task, a 100-step budget, thinking off unless stated, text only > (the vision tower is not served), sampling at temperature 0.8 with top-p 1.0 (the training sampling). Base model and > adapter always run under identical settings. These numbers are not comparable with the ones on the > [Qwen3.8-27B card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B), which uses other harnesses (Terminus, Claude Code), > thinking at maximum effort, larger budgets and the full SWE-bench Pro. Full recipe will be shared in [the release blogpost](https://huggingface.co/blog/harness-adapters-at-scale) for anyone to build their own harness adapter. **Pick your setup** [![Results](https://img.shields.io/badge/results-pass%401_%2B_efficiency-555?style=flat)](#results) [![transformers](https://img.shields.io/badge/serve-transformers-ffd21e?style=flat)](#use-with-transformers) [![vLLM](https://img.shields.io/badge/serve-vLLM-30A2FF?style=flat)](#use-with-pi) [![llama.cpp](https://img.shields.io/badge/run-llama.cpp-1f1f1f?style=flat)](#use-with-llama-cpp) [![Llama.app](https://img.shields.io/badge/macOS-Llama.app-7f7f7f?style=flat)](#run-with-llama-app) [![GGUF](https://img.shields.io/badge/download-GGUF-ff9d0b?style=flat)](https://huggingface.co/harness-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted-GGUF) [![Merge](https://img.shields.io/badge/merge-PEFT-ffd21e?style=flat)](#merge) [![Training](https://img.shields.io/badge/training-recipe-4b44c4?style=flat)](#training) [![Trajectories](https://img.shields.io/badge/trajectories-bucket-ff9d0b?style=flat)](#trajectories) A real SWE-bench Pro task under pi: the base model searches and re-runs snippets until it hits the 100-step limit; this adapter finds the function, edits it, runs the tests and fixes the last case, in 8 tool calls. ![](trajectory.gif)
Still version, and the task ![](trajectory.png) Task: `instance_ansible__ansible-d62496fe416623e88b90139dc7917080cb04ce70` from SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), fix `human_to_bytes`. Both runs are from the evaluation above: the base model was graded 0, this adapter 1. Each line is one tool call as the trajectory recorded it, cut to fit.
## Results ![](card-pi.png) | Benchmark | Qwen3.8-27B | Qwen3.8-27B, `xhigh` thinking | **Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted** | Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted, `xhigh` thinking | |---|---|---|---|---| | SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) | 39.2% | 74.5% | **64.7%** | 74.5% | | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | 41.0% | 54.2% | **56.6%** | 56.6% | On Terminal-Bench 2.1 the four runs are compared on the 83 tasks all of them graded, so the base model and adapter scores differ slightly from the paired results below, which use the 86 tasks those two graded. "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default reasoning effort (`xhigh`).
Full paired results (intervals and sign tests against the base model) One attempt per task, thinking off, paired against the base model under pi on the same tasks. The interval is 95%; the p-value is an exact sign test on the tasks that changed outcome. | Benchmark | Tasks | Qwen3.8-27B | Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted (step 160) | Difference (points) | Newly solved / lost | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) | 51 | 39.2% | 64.7% | +25.5 ± 14.2 | 15 / 2 (p = 0.0023) | | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | 86 | 39.5% | 55.8% | +16.3 ± 9.1 | 16 / 2 (p = 0.0013) | | Terminal-Bench 2.1, the 68 tasks not used to pick the checkpoint | 68 | 39.7% | 55.9% | +16.2 ± 10.6 | 13 / 2 (p = 0.0074) | - **SWE-bench Pro (hard 51):** the 51 hardest tasks of [SWE-bench Pro](https://huggingface.co/datasets/harness-hub/swebench-pro-v2-hard51-harbor), 2 h and 100 agent steps per task. - **Terminal-Bench 2.1:** all 89 tasks of [Terminal-Bench 2.1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/harborframework/terminal-bench-2.1), 1 h and 100 agent steps per task. Step 160 was picked by looking at the checkpoints' scores on SWE-bench Pro and on an 18-task subset of Terminal-Bench 2.1, tracked during training.
Work per solved task (turns, visible content, reasoning and generated tokens) Medians per task, this adapter / the base model, over the tasks both solved: same tasks, same outcome, so the numbers measure only how much work each needed. Generated tokens are everything the model writes (visible content, reasoning and tool calls); content is the visible text between tool calls. | | Tas

--- license: apache-2.0 language: - en - es - pt - de - fr - zh - ja - ru - ko pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio tags: - speech - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - haru --- # Haru-4B [Code](https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru) · [Technical blog](https://blog.higurashi.ai/melte/haru4b/) · [Technical blog (Japanese)](https://blog.higurashi.ai/melte/haru4b-ja/) Haru-4B is a low-latency and multilingual full-duplex continuous spoken dialogue foundation model: it listens and speaks at the same time, the way people do on a phone call. It is a pretrained base model, released for research. - **Native full-duplex at 7.5 Hz.** Every 133 ms the model takes one frame of the user's audio and produces one frame of its own audio and text. User audio, model audio and model text are summed into a single position of the language model, so listening and speaking never wait for each other. - **Continuous audio, one sampling step.** Audio is a 64-dimensional latent per frame. A small MLP head with MeanFlow sampling produces it in one step from the language model's hidden state; there is no separate audio transformer and there are no discrete audio tokens. - **Character and voice control.** A text card sets the character, a short reference clip sets the voice. - **Multilingual.** English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Chinese, Japanese, Russian and Korean.

## Usage The code is at : a PyTorch implementation with a web demo, an MLX implementation with a native macOS app, and a plugin for serving with vLLM-Omni. With an NVIDIA GPU (about 12 GB of memory): ```bash git clone https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru && cd Haru pip install -e ./haru python -m haru.server --hf-repo higurashi-ai/Haru-4B ``` Open , pick a character, give the model a voice, and talk. For low latency, we recommend wired headphones and a wired microphone. Bluetooth devices add 100 ms or more. **Bring your own voice.** Haru ships without voice clips. Upload or record a clip of the voice the model should speak with: one speaker, 3 seconds to 3 minutes, clean speech. Only use voices you have the right to use. ```python from haru import DuplexSession, HaruModel from haru.audio import load_audio, prepare_reference model = HaruModel.from_pretrained("higurashi-ai/Haru-4B") voice = prepare_reference(load_audio("voice.wav")) session = DuplexSession(model, system_prompt=card, reference=voice) frame = session.start() # the model's first 133 ms: frame.audio, frame.text while not frame.done: frame = session.step(user_audio) # 3200 samples at 24 kHz in, 3200 out ``` The system prompt is a character card with a fixed layout; the repository's README shows how to build one. ## Files | File | Contents | | --- | --- | | `model.safetensors` | All weights (bfloat16): `lm.*` language model, `model_audio_proj.*` / `user_audio_proj.*` audio input projections, `head.*` MeanFlow head, `codec.*` audio codec | | `config.json` | Model configuration | | `tokenizer.json` | Text tokenizer | ## Architecture | Part | Details | | --- | --- | | Language model | Qwen3.5-4B text backbone, 32 layers, hidden size 2560 | | Audio codec | VibeVoice acoustic tokenizer, causal, 24 kHz, 3200 samples per latent | | Audio head | 4-layer MLP, MeanFlow, 1 sampling step, guidance scale 1 to 2 (default 1.5) | | Frame rate | 7.5 Hz | ## Limitations Haru-4B is a pretrained base model, released for research. It holds a natural conversation, but it is not a reliable source of facts and does not follow instructions the way an assistant does. It can imitate the voice of a reference clip; only use voices you have the right to use. ## License The weights are released under the Apache License 2.0.

--- base_model: - meituan-longcat/LongCat-Video license: mit language: - en - zh library_name: longcat-video-avatar-1.6 tags: - audio-text-to-video - audio-image-text-to-video - audio-driven-video-continuation - diffusers - transformers - avatar - video-generation --- # LongCat-Video-Avatar-1.6
## 🚀 Model Introduction We are excited to announce the release of LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, the latest upgrade to our open-source framework for audio-driven human video generation. Building upon LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5, 1.6 improves expressive naturalness, lip–audio synchronization, coordinated facial and body motion, and visual consistency during long-form generation. It also introduces comprehensive inference optimizations for faster and more efficient deployment. ### Key Features - 🌟 **More Natural and Stable Lip Animation:**: Reduces exaggerated or strained mouth movements, overly red lip coloration, and temporal instability in the mouth region. - 🌟 **Stable Long-Video Generation**: Mitigates error accumulation during autoregressive video continuation, enabling videos exceeding 10 minutes while preserving visual quality, identity consistency, and temporal coherence. - 🌟 **Faster End-to-End Inference**: Accelerates video generation through end-to-end pipeline and model execution optimizations, enabling more efficient deployment and serving. For more detail, please refer to the comprehensive [***LongCat-Video-Avatar-1.6 Technical Report***](https://github.com/meituan-longcat/LongCat-Video/blob/main/assets/LongCat-Video-Avatar-1.6-Tech-Report.pdf). ## 🌀 Preview Gallery LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 delivers more natural lip movements and expressive motion while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency in videos exceeding 10 minutes.
## 📊 Human Evaluation We compare LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 with its predecessor LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 and four commercial systems: OmniHuman-2.0, HeyGen, OmniHuman-1.5, and Kling Avatar 2.0. The all-pairs human preference study comprises 33,051 valid individual votes across all 15 model pairings. LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 ranks second among six evaluated systems in a human preference Arena comprising 33,051 valid individual votes. With a Bradley–Terry Elo score of 1068.1, it ranks behind OmniHuman-2.0 and ahead of LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5, HeyGen, OmniHuman-1.5, and Kling Avatar 2.0.
## 💡 Quick Start Clone the repo ```shell git clone --single-branch --branch main https://github.com/meituan-longcat/LongCat-Video cd LongCat-Video ``` Install dependencies ```shell # create conda environment conda create -n longcat-video python=3.10 conda activate longcat-video # install torch (configure according to your CUDA version) pip install torch==2.6.0+cu124 torchvision==0.21.0+cu124 torchaudio==2.6.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124 # install flash-attn-2 pip install ninja pip install psutil pip install packaging pip install flash_attn==2.7.4.post1 # install other requirements pip install -r requirements.txt # install longcat-video-avatar requirements conda install -c conda-forge librosa conda install -c c

# tiny-voca

tiny-voca is a small English text-to-speech model with two voices, F2 (female)
and M2 (male). The complete model, including the waveform generator, has 4.5M
parameters and was trained from scratch on about 18 hours of synthetic speech.
It runs about 70x faster than real time on four CPU threads.

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/F2-1.wav"></audio>

- Code: https://github.com/n4ze3m/tiny-voca
- Phonemizer: https://github.com/n4ze3m/dizione
- Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/n4ze3m/tiny-voca
- Try it in the browser: https://huggingface.co/spaces/n4ze3m/tiny-voca-studio

| | |
|---|---|
| Parameters | 4,537,291 |
| Voices | F2, M2 (American English) |
| Output | 24 kHz mono |
| Input | Text, converted to phonemes with dizione |
| Pretrained weights in the model | None |
| License | Apache-2.0 |

## Files

| File | Size | Contents |
|---|---:|---|
| `tiny-voca.pt` | 18.2 MB | PyTorch weights, float32 |
| `onnx/model.onnx` | 21.4 MB | ONNX export, float32, opset 17 |
| `config.json` | | Model settings, phoneme vocabulary, voices |
| `phonemizer/` | 5.4 MB | Data files for dizione |
| `samples/` | | The audio on this page |

SHA256:

- `tiny-voca.pt`: `ebb22871524c5732520fb1652e6aefcec708a7452e83bdd00adcf6181db5ef70`
- `onnx/model.onnx`: `fe6d918791a15b82e37465981d7f27a070e46b46635e5a3482fc8dff87a1ae46`

## Samples

| Text | F2 | M2 |
|---|---|---|
| Hello! This is tiny voca, a small text to speech model that runs on a phone or in a browser. | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/F2-1.wav"></audio> | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/M2-1.wav"></audio> |
| The meeting moved to 3:30 pm on March 14th, so we have about 45 minutes left. | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/F2-2.wav"></audio> | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/M2-2.wav"></audio> |
| Did you really think I would forget your birthday? | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/F2-3.wav"></audio> | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/M2-3.wav"></audio> |
| She had never seen the sea before, and for a long while she stood at the edge of the water without saying a word. | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/F2-4.wav"></audio> | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/n4ze3m/tiny-voca/resolve/main/samples/M2-4.wav"></audio> |

## Usage

### PyTorch

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/n4ze3m/dizione git+https://github.com/n4ze3m/tiny-voca
hf download n4ze3m/tiny-voca --local-dir tiny-voca
export DIZIONE_DATA=tiny-voca/phonemizer

python -m tiny_voca.infer \
  --checkpoint tiny-voca/tiny-voca.pt \
  --voice F2 \
  --text "Hello! This is tiny voca." \
  --output hello.wav
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--text-file` | | Read the text from a file instead of `--text`. |
| `--voice` | `F2` | `F2` or `M2` |
| `--speed` | 1.0 | Speaking rate |
| `--pitch-shift` | 0 | Added to log F0. 0.058 is about one semitone. |
| `--pitch-range` | 1.0 | Scales pitch movement around the utterance mean. |

Text of any length works. The command reads it one sentence at a time and
joins the audio. A text that ends without a mark gets a full stop. A sentence
with nothing to read, such as one in another script, is skipped. The saved
audio never peaks above 0.99.

### ONNX

The graph takes phoneme ids and stress values and returns the waveform. Text is
converted to ids outside the graph with dizione; the ids are the positions in
`vocab` in `config.json`.

```python
import numpy as np
import onnxruntime as ort
import soundfile as sf
import dizione   # needs DIZIONE_DATA=tiny-voca/phonemizer

phones = dizione.phonemize("Hello! This is tiny voca.")
one = lambda value: np.array([value], dtype=np.float32)

session = ort.InferenceSession("tiny-voca/onnx/model.onnx")
audio, durations = session.run(None, {
    "tokens": np.array([phones.ids], dtype=np.int64),
    "stress": np.array([phones.stress], dtype=np.int64),
    "voice": np.array([0], dtype=np.int64),      # 0 = F2, 1 = M2
    "speed": one(1.0),
    "pitch_shift": one(0.0),
    "pitch_range": one(1.0),
})
audio = audio[0]
audio = audio * min(1.0, 0.99 / np.abs(audio).max())    # the model can peak above 1.0
sf.write("hello.wav", audio, 24000)
```

| Input | Type | Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tokens` | int64 | [1, N] | Phoneme ids, including the start and end tokens |
| `stress` | int64 | [1, N] | 0 none, 1 primary, 2 secondary |
| `voice` | int64 | [1] | 0 = F2, 1 = M2 |
| `speed` | float32 | [1] | 1.0 as predicted; larger is faster |
| `pitch_shift` | float32 | [1] | Added to log F0 |
| `pitch_range` | float32 | [1] | Scales pitch movement |

| Output | Type | Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `audio` | float32 | [1, samples] | Waveform at 24 kHz |
| `durations` | int64 | [1, N] | Length of each token in frames of 256 samples |

The model reads one utterance per call, up to 512 tokens and 32 seconds. Split
longer text into sentences; `tiny_voca.infer.speak_text` does this in Python.
End each utterance with a mark such as a full stop: without one the last word
breaks off.
The audio can peak a little above 1.0 (about one sentence in twenty), so scale
it down before you save 16-bit samples, as above. The same file runs in
onnxruntime-web (WebAssembly). Its audio matches the PyTorch model to within
0.6% of the peak amplitude, apart from the random noise signal, which each
runtime draws itself.

## Model

Text is converted to phonemes with a s
